SS-214   /   DIESEL–ELECTRIC PATROL BOAT
QUIET DEPTHS / FIRST PATROL

A little courage.
A lot of listening.

An ocean you can’t see through. A boat with limits. A few consequential decisions before bed.

PATROL CONDITIONS

Day turns to night during your patrol. Clear skies, rain and storms change how far either side can see.

YOUR FIRST ORDERS

Look through the scope and photograph the convoy. Dive to disappear. Use the chart and time compression to get home. Esc pauses everything.

HEADPHONES RECOMMENDED · SAVES ON THIS DEVICE
 THE CAPTAIN’S FIELD GUIDE

Be hard to find.

01 / Listen

Passive sonar gives you a bearing, not a location. The chart draws an uncertain line. An active ping estimates range, but alerts nearby hunters. Contact estimates age; they are never a live enemy map.

02 / Take a look

At 15 meters or less, raise the scope. Drag to turn, scroll to zoom. Looking identifies ships and estimates range. Photograph merchant silhouettes with F. The scope angle is relative to the hull, so the view turns with the boat. Fishing boats are neutral. A scope and a surfaced hull can be spotted.

03 / Stay alive

Electric is quiet; diesel needs 14 meters or less and recharges air and battery. R limits speed to 3 knots. Deep water muffles you, but 220 meters is test depth. Chart contours show reefs; keep water under your keel.

04 / Leave quietly

Select a contact to fire a homing torpedo. It seeks a loud target in its forward cone and may choose badly. Escorts hunt noise and drop charges. Turn, dive, release a noisemaker. Damage control slowly patches the hull and flooding at a battery cost.

05 / Borrow another pair of eyes

Deploy your inspection drone at 280 meters or less, while the boat is at 3 knots or less. Keep within 100 meters in three dimensions; link loss is permanent for the patrol. W/S change requested speed, A/D requested heading, Space requested depth toward the surface, and C deeper. The camera stays fixed dead ahead. The helm shows actual and requested values; the vehicle responds gradually. A 10% alarm warns of low drone battery. Return before it runs out. Docking charges the drone and repairs its hull, camera, thrusters and buoyancy. Electric charging uses some boat battery; diesel supplies it directly. Your boat keeps its orders while you’re away.

06 / A patrol before bed

Choose 5× or 20× for travel. New contacts and attacks return you to 1×. Drag the chart to pan and use the wheel to zoom. Click to plot a waypoint; requested depth stays yours to manage. After your task, return to the green extraction circle and surface for pickup. While paused, helm and mission actions are disabled. Esc pauses; progress autosaves locally.

Read the water beneath you

Helm depth is measured from mean sea level. Water depth runs from the surface to the seabed. Below Keel is the space under your hull, accounting for its five-meter radius. The drone station shows clearance below the drone. Shallow clearance is highlighted.

Use the weather

Choose a starting time and weather before a new patrol. Night and storms shorten visual detection range; running lights can still betray ships beyond silhouette range. Rough seas can wash over your lens. A full environmental day takes 48 simulated minutes. Changing fronts develop gradually.

Listen for the flash

Lightning has a location. Thunder follows after sound travels to your moving boat. Submerged thunder is quieter and muffled further with depth. Pausing freezes sound arrivals; time compression speeds their travel through game time.

Hear traffic and trouble

Enable Sound to hear nearby engines grow louder as you close and pan as you turn. Depth charges sink to their fuse depth, detonate, and send out a pressure front. Nearby explosions produce louder, sharper shocks; distant ones rumble. Changing course and depth before detonation can save you.

Rescue and survey

Plot the marked mission site with PLOT APPROACH. The boat stops beside it at the requested rescue depth. Undersea rescue needs 30–75 m separation, the stated depth ±5 m and ≤0.6 kn. Surface rescue needs 30–85 m and depth under 1 m. Hold for assessment, survivor transfers and the team’s return. Survivor counts start unknown and can fall with time. Survey at 0.5–3 kn within 100 m and 32 m of wreck depth for 45 seconds, or take three drone photographs from sides at least 55° apart.

A boat with consequences

Ballast changes buoyancy even at all stop. Moving dive planes add lift. Floodwater weighs the boat down; pumps and repair crew must keep up. Open Subsystem Condition to inspect damage. A lost periscope stays lost, but the conning tower gives a wide view when fully surfaced. Drag vertically there to look down at your deck. The drone and wrecks have solid hulls. Shallow, fast propellers cavitate, making visible vapor and more noise.
